Phrases in Combination: Practice for Chapter 13

Chapter 13 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom with real tunes: perfect and imperfect authentic cadences, the sentence, periods (parallel and contrasting), repeated phrases and periods, and where to hear the rest.

This page goes with Chapter 13, Phrases in Combination of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first. Chapter 11 showed what a phrase is; this chapter asks how two or more phrases fit together, and the answer is nearly always in the cadences. The examples are tunes from the site’s own Tune Library, played by the band with the chords written in. Press ▶ on each one, then look at the chord and the melody note at the end of every four-bar phrase.

How to read a phrase’s ending: find the last chord of the phrase and the melody note on it. Two chords before it help (V or V7 into I). The cadence labels below were read from the chord symbols in the collection, so check them by ear too. The answer to “is this really a cadence?” depends on the arrangement.

13.1 Perfect and imperfect authentic cadences

Chapter 7 gave you the authentic cadence (V or V7 to I). Chapter 13 splits it in two. A perfect authentic cadence (PAC) needs all three of these: both chords in root position, the tonic chord last, and scale degree 1 in the top voice of that last chord. Break any one of them (a chord inverted, or the melody ending on 3 or 5 instead) and it is an imperfect authentic cadence (IAC). Read 13.1

In a tune with chord symbols the melody note is easy to see. Both phrases of this line end V7 to I in the key of G:

TipAnswer

Bar 4: D7 to G, melody on B (scale degree 3), so an IAC. Bar 8: D7 to G, melody on G (scale degree 1), so a PAC. The chords are the same; only the top note differs, and the second ending sounds more finished.

13.2 The sentence

A sentence is a phrase with a particular shape. It starts with an idea (a motive or a two-bar subphrase), then the idea comes again, repeated or sequenced (moved up or down), perhaps with its intervals bent to fit the new chord. What follows is different: related or new material that moves faster and drives to the cadence. A sentence is one phrase, so it ends in a cadence. It can be the first or the second phrase of a period. Read 13.2

Here is one made for this page (not a famous tune), eight bars. Bars 1-2 are the idea, bars 3-4 the idea again on the dominant chord with its notes changed to fit, bars 5-8 the continuation: a two-note fragment, then a scalewise run, then V7 to I.

TipAnswer

Idea: bar 1 (an arpeggio up and back, then a rest-filled hold in bar 2). Repetition: bar 3, the same shape on G7, with bar 4 holding again. Continuation: bar 5 breaks the idea into a two-note fragment, bar 6 runs down a scale, bars 7-8 close V7 to I with the melody on 1: a PAC. The four bars of continuation are faster than the four bars of presentation; that “speeding up” is what you listen for.

Where to hear real ones. The book analyses sentences in Mozart’s Piano Sonata K. 331, I, Beethoven’s Piano Sonata Op. 2 No. 1, I, and the second theme of Mozart’s K. 333, I. Two of those are in the site’s Analysed Scores Library, where you can follow the score with the analysis under it: Beethoven, Op. 2 No. 1, movement 1 (the opening eight bars) and Mozart, K. 333, movement 1. The Classical Themes page has more themes to try the test on: does the second idea repeat the first, and does the music speed up before the cadence?

13.3 The period

A period is two or more phrases where the last cadence is more conclusive than the first. The book gives two usual pairs: a half cadence (HC) then an authentic cadence (IAC or PAC); or an IAC then a PAC. The first phrase (the less conclusive ending) is the antecedent, the question; the second is the consequent, the answer. Read 13.3

HC then PAC. Both phrases of “Skip to My Lou” begin the same way. The first ends on F7, the V chord; the second ends on B♭.

IAC then PAC. “London Bridge” shows the other pair. Bar 4 is V7 to I, but the melody is on F (scale degree 5); bar 8 puts the tonic in the melody.

TipAnswers and what to notice

“Skip to My Lou”: HC (bar 4, melody on the E♭, the seventh of F7), then PAC (bar 8, B♭ in the melody). “London Bridge”: IAC (bar 4, F in the melody), then PAC (bar 8, B♭ low in the melody). Both are parallel periods: the two phrases begin the same (13.4). Sing the first phrase and stop; it should feel as if someone has asked a question.

13.4 Parallel and contrasting periods

If both phrases begin with the same melody, the period is parallel. If they begin differently, it is contrasting. A phrase that looks like an earlier one but ends with a different cadence gets a prime: a, then a′. (“Skip to My Lou” and “London Bridge” are a a′.) The prime marks a different ending, not an ornamented melody. Read 13.4

The chorus of “O Susanna” is contrasting: its first four bars (starting on A♭, the IV chord) are new, and they end on B♭7, the dominant. The next four-bar phrase brings back the tune of the verse and settles on E♭.

TipAnswer

Phrase 1 (bars 1-4) ends on B♭7 with the melody on F: HC. Phrase 2 (bars 5-8) ends B♭7 to E♭ with the melody on E♭: PAC. The phrases begin differently, so this is a contrasting period, labelled b a with HC and PAC. (The a here is the same tune as the verse’s phrases. The letters are about the melody, so they follow the tune, not the order.)

13.5 Repeated phrases and repeated periods

Two things to watch when you see a phrase twice.

  • Repeated phrase: the same phrase twice with the same cadence. Two phrases with the same ending are not a period, because the second is not more conclusive. “Long, Long Ago” is a case: both four-bar lines end V7 to I with 1 on top (the second only dresses the last bar differently).
  • Repeated period: four phrases, but the cadence after the second phrase is already a PAC. That is two periods in a row, not a double period.

“Little Brown Jug” (13.1) has four phrases whose endings are IAC, PAC, IAC, PAC. The PAC halfway through ends the first period, so the whole tune is a repeated period. The verse of “O Susanna” is the same: HC, PAC, HC, PAC.

TipAnswer

Both endings are V7 to I with scale degree 1 in the melody (bar 4 on the low B♭ after a step down; bar 8 the same): two PACs. The second phrase is not more conclusive, so this is not a period. It does have a different tune in the second phrase (F-F-E-D…), so it is not a repeated phrase either. The book does not name every combination, and this is a good example of how a pair of phrases can fall outside its labels.

13.6 Asymmetrical and double periods

An asymmetrical period has three or five phrases, so there are unequal numbers of antecedents and consequents (one question, two answers). A double period has four or more phrases in two groups: an antecedent group (phrases 1-2) whose last cadence is the inconclusive one, and a consequent group (phrases 3-4) that ends with a more conclusive cadence. The usual melodic scheme is a b a b′. If the cadence in the middle is already a PAC, you have a repeated period instead (13.5). Read 13.6

These need longer pieces than a folk song, so they are best met in the library:

  • Double period: Mozart, Piano Sonata K. 333, I, second theme, which the book analyses as a parallel double period with a PAC at the end (K. 333, movement 1).
  • Contrasting period in a slow movement: Beethoven, Pathétique Sonata, II (Op. 13, movement 2), the book’s example of a contrasting period.

Open the library’s score, find the theme, and use the Roman numerals under the staff to label each phrase ending.

13.7 Phrase groups, phrase chains and elision

If a series of phrases ends on a half cadence, it is not a period. When the phrases begin alike it is a phrase group; when they start differently, a phrase chain. (The book takes these terms from Douglass Green.) An elision is the overlap where the last bar of one phrase is also the first bar of the next, so the bar count is one fewer than the phrases add up to. Read 13.7

No tune in the site’s folk collection is a clean example of either; examples from keyboard pieces are in 13.9 below. The book uses Couperin and a Beethoven rondo. To practise elision, count the bars of each phrase in a tune you know and see whether the numbers add up to the total.

13.8 Putting it together

For each excerpt, in this order (the book’s own routine):

  1. Label the chords at the end of each phrase with Roman numerals and name the cadence (PAC, IAC, HC, PC, DC).
  2. Look at the melody: is a phrase a sentence?
  3. Write a diagram: letters for the melody (a, a′, b), the cadence under each.
  4. Name the form: sentence, parallel or contrasting period, asymmetrical period, parallel double period, repeated phrase, or repeated period.

Try it on the tunes in the Tune Library: “Yankee Doodle” (its verse and refrain), “Oh! Susanna” as a whole, “Simple Gifts”, “America”. The book’s own practice excerpts (Mozart’s “Ein Mädchen oder Weibchen”, K. 333 I, and Dédé’s Chicago) are under copyright or need the book’s scores, so they are not reproduced here; the answers are in the book’s exercise section.

13.9 Keyboard pieces in the full-score library

Some of the book’s own examples (and pieces like them) are in the site’s full-score player. The readings below come from the notes (bar numbers count a pickup as bar 1), checked against the bass line for the chords; they are unverified by a printed edition or a recording, and the scores are community engravings.

  • A parallel period: Beethoven, Für Elise (open the score). The first phrase ends in bar 4 on the E major chord (V of A minor) with B in the melody: a half cadence. Bar 5 is an A minor bar, and the second phrase repeats the opening (bars 6-7 are bars 2-3 note for note) and ends in bar 9 on A over an A minor chord, after E in the bass in bar 8: a perfect authentic cadence. The phrases begin the same, so it is a parallel period, a a′ with HC and PAC. The second phrase is a bar longer than the first, because of the tonic bar 5. The book analyses this same piece as its period example.
  • A phrase chain (my reading): Anh. 115 Minuet in G minor (open the score). Bars 1-4 end on D in the bass with a D major chord (V of G minor), and bars 5-8 end the same way (A in the melody over D, after F♯ in the bass): two phrases with different openings, both ending on half cadences. By the book’s definition that is a phrase chain, because the group ends on an HC and the phrases begin differently. It is two phrases, the smallest chain there can be.
  • A phrase chain from the book: Beethoven, Sonatina in F, Anh. 5 No. 2, Rondo (open the score). The book names this rondo’s refrain as its phrase-chain example. In the score, the refrain (bars 1-18) has phrase endings around bars 4, 8 and 12 and then a longer last phrase that ends in bar 18 on a C chord (V of F). The openings differ: three repeated F notes in bar 1, the same figure a step higher in bar 5, new tunes in bars 9 and 13. Check the cadence on bar 18 by ear.

Still missing from the collection: an asymmetrical period (three or five phrases) and an elision that I could confirm from the notes. I looked at the Bach notebook minuets, polonaises, the musette and the gavotte, and each is in two- or four-phrase groups or too thickly decorated to call without hearing. A bar-numbered reading of a classical piano score would settle it.

NoteFor teachers
  • Sources of the examples: the six folk tunes are from the site’s tune collection (the recorder teacher’s-guide set and the beginning-band set). Only the sentence is original to this page; it was checked for bar length by script and is meant as a clear model, not a quotation.
  • The cadence labels were read from the chord symbols in the collection, not from a score or a recording. A teacher may hear some of them differently (for example, whether the first phrase of “Go Tell Aunt Rhody” is a PAC or a weaker close because the melody lands on the low B♭).
  • Keyboard pieces (13.9): the cadences were read from the melody and bass notes of the PDMX-derived scores (apps/shared/data/full-scores/pdmx-<n>.abc). Für Elise is the book’s own example; the Anh. 115 minuet is this page’s reading and may be argued. The Sonatina refrain is the book’s named phrase chain, and the bar numbers are from the score.
  • Not covered here: an asymmetrical period and an elision (none confirmed from the notes), phrase groups (none found), and the book’s analyses of Beethoven Op. 2 No. 1, Mozart K. 331 and K. 333 with bar numbers (the library’s bar numbers have not been matched to the book’s figures).
